elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause after 9.3: "Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience on thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor." This covers both the Agreement and any Order Form.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted sentence sets the notice at "thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor," i.e. no more than 30 days, and it is written notice.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: The only refund language is retained 10.2: "Vendor shall refund prepaid recurring Fees covering the period after termination." That is a post-termination-period refund, not an express pro-rata refund, and it is confined to prepaid *recurring* Fees rather than prepaid Fees generally (e.g. prepaid professional services or usage Fees). The new 9.4 adds no refund mechanic.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Inserted second sentence: "Vendor may not terminate this Agreement or an Order Form for convenience during a committed term." Sections 9.1–9.3 give Vendor only for-cause and insolvency rights, so no contrary retained language exists.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The rendered right is on "thirty days' prior written notice," which is outside the stated 60–90 day fallback band; no 60–90 day notice term appears anywhere.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither Section 9, the inserted clause, nor 10.2 imposes any early-termination fee or penalty on Customer's exit, so there is no fee requiring a cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The inserted sentence bars Vendor convenience termination "during a committed term," and no other clause grants Vendor a convenience right, so any such right could only arise outside a committed term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Vendor holds no convenience termination right at all under 9.1–9.3 as amended, so no Vendor convenience notice period is engaged.

reasons: Preferred level is incomplete on one element only: the pro-rata refund. Retained 10.2 promises a refund of "prepaid recurring Fees covering the period after termination" — a post-termination-period refund is not the same as an express pro-rata refund, and "recurring Fees" is narrower than prepaid Fees as defined in 1.5 (which also includes professional services and usage fees). Repair by adding to the new convenience clause: "...in which case Vendor shall refund, on a pro-rata basis, all prepaid Fees covering the period after the effective date of termination."

Fallback level is incomplete because the drafted notice period (30 days) does not fall within the 60–90 day band; the fallback is therefore unavailable as an alternative complete position, and the redline must be finished at the preferred level by adding the pro-rata refund language.

Minimality is satisfied: the insertion is two sentences confined to the checklist (Customer convenience right, 30-day notice, no Vendor convenience right), correctly omits the model language's surplus "in whole or in part," adds no survival, expense or procedural tails, and deletes no existing words. Sections 9.1–9.3, 9.5 and 10.2 are retained intact.

Intent is preserved: 8.1's three-year term is expressly subject to earlier termination "in accordance with its terms," 9.5's non-cascade and cumulative-remedies language still operates on the new right, and no cross-reference or defined term is left dangling.

Drafting fix (non-substantive): the inserted paragraph is rendered without a clause number and sits between 9.3 and 9.5; label it "9.4" so the numbering sequence and any future cross-references remain coherent.
